compare_blocks.body:
In a reputational incident both may have said "hold off publishing", and both will pull up what has already gone out to check it. That resemblance is easily remembered as the same kind of steadiness, when it comes more from the shared J and from the post — anyone sitting in an outward-facing role, of any type, will be asked to think before speaking.

The shared J only says both tend to form an arrangement outward; it does not say what the arrangement is built on. The three differences are read separately: E/I is whether attention and energy turn outward or inward more often; S/N is whether sourcing trusts facts and experience, or notices connections and possibility faster; T/F is whether the judgement weighs a consistently applicable standard, or people and values. The three cannot substitute for each other, and "who moves first" cannot stand in for any of them.

### The same negative comment, two usable entry points

In this fictional example, a widely shared post says a product broke after two months and customer support failed to help. The company has full support records and can deliver a resolution within three days.

One entry point is the checkable record: which order this user placed, how long the first support reply took, what result can be delivered within how many days. The other looks for patterns across the replies: are people reporting a product fault, feeling dismissed by support, or both? This illustrates an S/N contrast in the use of information. Either person can check the records and look for recurring concerns, and neither approach identifies someone’s type.

Both entry points have costs. Checking only the facts may produce a statement read as a work report, with the anger intact; reading only the feeling may promise what cannot be delivered. A workable order is to spend an hour confirming what can be checked, then use those facts to calibrate the tone; the two do not need two people, and who does which part follows the information, authority and duty at the time.

Order is not a criterion. An ESTJ who has worked support or communications may weigh tone first, and an INFJ who has handled many incidents may pull the timeline first; the reverse is also common. The scene shows which kind of basis each cites more often; it does not show who cares more about people.

### No position shares a name — what is shared is the four kinds of process

In the four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se: ESTJ leads with Te, auxiliary Si, third Ne, inferior Fi; INFJ leads with Ni, auxiliary Fe, third Ti, inferior Se. No position shares a name.

Both stacks include Thinking, Feeling, Sensing and Intuition. The exact labels differ because each function is directed inward in one stack and outward in the other, and the order also changes: ESTJ puts judging outward (Te) and perceiving inward (Si); INFJ integrates perceptually inward first (Ni) and judges outward (Fe).

What each position more often handles: Te writes standards and results into an executable, checkable form; Si compares the present situation with past experience and precedent; Ne moves from one thing to other explanations and other possibilities; Fi lets a judgement carry the values one holds. Ni integrates scattered clues into a pattern or a direction; Fe reads the feelings of those present and the shared understanding between them; Ti checks whether a set of statements is internally consistent; Se takes the facts available to the senses right now.

Whether the third position is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables: for ESTJ's Ne and INFJ's Ti, some tables give only the function name without settling an attitude. This page uses the common writing and does not present it as the Foundation's only version; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain who cares more about others. A position is an emphasis in the model, and does not show who is better at which kind of work, whether a collaboration runs smoothly, or who attracts whom. compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
Scope note: what follows is how the two organise information and divide the work inside one fictional incident. It does not cover legal characterisation, crisis-handling procedure or the specific scale of a public commitment. Anything touching the law is for legal counsel; when a public line is needed, follow the company's approval and compliance process.

Working together, the two easily get stuck where there is no agreement on what is actually being solved, and the statement has already gone out. That is usually a matter of collaborative rhythm, not of type pairing.

The division is assigned by authority, experience and current duty, and either type can do any part: fact-checking, the limits of a commitment, wording and follow-up communication all need a second pair of eyes. When publication needs delaying, write down three things: what is still being checked, the latest point at which a decision must be made, and whether a short progress note should go out first.

### A public reply to one negative comment

(Fictional scene.) The same matter admits two equally acceptable pieces of writing. One sets out the check results and the actions: when the user bought, that the first reply took more than forty-eight hours, that a replacement has been arranged with shipping refunded, and that the response time limit now sits in performance reviews. The other acknowledges the situation first: that a user was only heard after being passed around repeatedly is itself a failure, and a replacement is only the floor.

The first offers an account that can be checked; the second offers an attitude that can be believed. Publish only the first and readers know the process changed while the anger remains; only the second and readers find it agreeable but cannot tell what actually changed. Either type can write either version; the difference is which kind of basis is thought of first.

The check can be a read-through: show both versions to a few readers outside the company and ask three questions each — which facts did you see, which commitment did you remember, and do you think the other side's dissatisfaction was answered. The feedback reports the effect of the text; it does not verify the writer's type or function preference, and cannot show who is better suited to writing statements.

### A friend is being piled on in the comments

(Fictional scene.) A friend's opinion trends and the comments are full of personal attacks. What can be done falls into two kinds: operational — do not reply yet, save screenshots, appeal to the platform if needed, put together a timeline; and companionable — call first, let them talk it out, then ask "do you want me to say something publicly".

Both can go wrong: only the operational makes the person feel alone, and only the comforting leaves the actual harm continuing. Either type may do either first, and either may do both.

A workable move is to ask the friend which kind of help they want, and to make "I will not speak for you" an explicit option. Speaking for someone looks loyal but can spread the fire to two people; whether to respond publicly is the person's own decision.

### New material appears late at night

(Fictional scene.) Four hours after the statement goes out, someone posts a recording of a support call whose tone is worse than the written record. Three pieces of information work can be done: obtain the full recording, confirm whether it was edited, and judge whether it is a new fact or new evidence of the same fact.

The nature changes where the reply lands: if it is a new fact, acknowledge first that this was not known, then add; if it is new evidence of the same fact, the point is why it was not stated clearly before. If the deadline is already tight and media are pressing, either type may put out a short note first and fill in detail later. The most common failure in a panic is meeting feeling with process language — that has nothing to do with type and everything to do with how prepared you were.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
"Who is more decisive" cannot be evidence. ESTJ decides fast when information is complete and authority is clear, and INFJ is equally unhurried when the direction is clear; conversely, both are cautious when the facts are unclear. Speed is a product of circumstance and experience.

"Who is colder" is also a misreading. ESTJ's Fi sitting fourth does not mean not caring about people, only that it is not often the first basis for a judgement; INFJ's Fe sitting second, in the auxiliary, does not mean having no principles. A position describes emphasis, not how much anyone cares.

The third misread is taking J as a need to control or a short temper. J describes forming an arrangement outward first; it is not the same as telling others what to do, and not the same as deciding faster. Reading organisation as dominance and empathy as weakness turns a preference into a character judgement.

The fourth is settling a type from one performance. "Check facts first" and "read the feeling first" can both appear in either type, and the same person switches sides in different settings. Classifying on one sighting usually gets it wrong.

The fifth is taking a job for a type. People in support, communications or incident response are trained into a fixed set of moves; that is the result of training, not a change of preference.

body: In a reputational incident both may have said "hold off publishing", and both will pull up what has already gone out to check it. That resemblance is easily remembered as the same kind of steadiness, when it comes more from the shared J and from the post — anyone sitting in an outward-facing role, of any type, will be asked to think before speaking.

The shared J only says both tend to form an arrangement outward; it does not say what the arrangement is built on. The three differences are read separately: E/I is whether attention and energy turn outward or inward more often; S/N is whether sourcing trusts facts and experience, or notices connections and possibility faster; T/F is whether the judgement weighs a consistently applicable standard, or people and values. The three cannot substitute for each other, and "who moves first" cannot stand in for any of them.
### The same negative comment, two usable entry points

In this fictional example, a widely shared post says a product broke after two months and customer support failed to help. The company has full support records and can deliver a resolution within three days.

One entry point is the checkable record: which order this user placed, how long the first support reply took, what result can be delivered within how many days. The other looks for patterns across the replies: are people reporting a product fault, feeling dismissed by support, or both? This illustrates an S/N contrast in the use of information. Either person can check the records and look for recurring concerns, and neither approach identifies someone’s type.

Both entry points have costs. Checking only the facts may produce a statement read as a work report, with the anger intact; reading only the feeling may promise what cannot be delivered. A workable order is to spend an hour confirming what can be checked, then use those facts to calibrate the tone; the two do not need two people, and who does which part follows the information, authority and duty at the time.

Order is not a criterion. An ESTJ who has worked support or communications may weigh tone first, and an INFJ who has handled many incidents may pull the timeline first; the reverse is also common. The scene shows which kind of basis each cites more often; it does not show who cares more about people.
### No position shares a name — what is shared is the four kinds of process

In the four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se: ESTJ leads with Te, auxiliary Si, third Ne, inferior Fi; INFJ leads with Ni, auxiliary Fe, third Ti, inferior Se. No position shares a name.

Both stacks include Thinking, Feeling, Sensing and Intuition. The exact labels differ because each function is directed inward in one stack and outward in the other, and the order also changes: ESTJ puts judging outward (Te) and perceiving inward (Si); INFJ integrates perceptually inward first (Ni) and judges outward (Fe).

What each position more often handles: Te writes standards and results into an executable, checkable form; Si compares the present situation with past experience and precedent; Ne moves from one thing to other explanations and other possibilities; Fi lets a judgement carry the values one holds. Ni integrates scattered clues into a pattern or a direction; Fe reads the feelings of those present and the shared understanding between them; Ti checks whether a set of statements is internally consistent; Se takes the facts available to the senses right now.

Whether the third position is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables: for ESTJ's Ne and INFJ's Ti, some tables give only the function name without settling an attitude. This page uses the common writing and does not present it as the Foundation's only version; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain who cares more about others. A position is an emphasis in the model, and does not show who is better at which kind of work, whether a collaboration runs smoothly, or who attracts whom. Both base descriptions are the [ESTJ profile](/en/personality/estj) and the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj).

body: Scope note: what follows is how the two organise information and divide the work inside one fictional incident. It does not cover legal characterisation, crisis-handling procedure or the specific scale of a public commitment. Anything touching the law is for legal counsel; when a public line is needed, follow the company's approval and compliance process.

Working together, the two easily get stuck where there is no agreement on what is actually being solved, and the statement has already gone out. That is usually a matter of collaborative rhythm, not of type pairing.

The division is assigned by authority, experience and current duty, and either type can do any part: fact-checking, the limits of a commitment, wording and follow-up communication all need a second pair of eyes. When publication needs delaying, write down three things: what is still being checked, the latest point at which a decision must be made, and whether a short progress note should go out first.
### A public reply to one negative comment

(Fictional scene.) The same matter admits two equally acceptable pieces of writing. One sets out the check results and the actions: when the user bought, that the first reply took more than forty-eight hours, that a replacement has been arranged with shipping refunded, and that the response time limit now sits in performance reviews. The other acknowledges the situation first: that a user was only heard after being passed around repeatedly is itself a failure, and a replacement is only the floor.

The first offers an account that can be checked; the second offers an attitude that can be believed. Publish only the first and readers know the process changed while the anger remains; only the second and readers find it agreeable but cannot tell what actually changed. Either type can write either version; the difference is which kind of basis is thought of first.

The check can be a read-through: show both versions to a few readers outside the company and ask three questions each — which facts did you see, which commitment did you remember, and do you think the other side's dissatisfaction was answered. The feedback reports the effect of the text; it does not verify the writer's type or function preference, and cannot show who is better suited to writing statements.
### A friend is being piled on in the comments

(Fictional scene.) A friend's opinion trends and the comments are full of personal attacks. What can be done falls into two kinds: operational — do not reply yet, save screenshots, appeal to the platform if needed, put together a timeline; and companionable — call first, let them talk it out, then ask "do you want me to say something publicly".
Both can go wrong: only the operational makes the person feel alone, and only the comforting leaves the actual harm continuing. Either type may do either first, and either may do both.

A workable move is to ask the friend which kind of help they want, and to make "I will not speak for you" an explicit option. Speaking for someone looks loyal but can spread the fire to two people; whether to respond publicly is the person's own decision.
### New material appears late at night

(Fictional scene.) Four hours after the statement goes out, someone posts a recording of a support call whose tone is worse than the written record. Three pieces of information work can be done: obtain the full recording, confirm whether it was edited, and judge whether it is a new fact or new evidence of the same fact.

The nature changes where the reply lands: if it is a new fact, acknowledge first that this was not known, then add; if it is new evidence of the same fact, the point is why it was not stated clearly before. If the deadline is already tight and media are pressing, either type may put out a short note first and fill in detail later. The most common failure in a panic is meeting feeling with process language — that has nothing to do with type and everything to do with how prepared you were.

body: "Who is more decisive" cannot be evidence. ESTJ decides fast when information is complete and authority is clear, and INFJ is equally unhurried when the direction is clear; conversely, both are cautious when the facts are unclear. Speed is a product of circumstance and experience.

"Who is colder" is also a misreading. ESTJ's Fi sitting fourth does not mean not caring about people, only that it is not often the first basis for a judgement; INFJ's Fe sitting second, in the auxiliary, does not mean having no principles. A position describes emphasis, not how much anyone cares.

The third misread is taking J as a need to control or a short temper. J describes forming an arrangement outward first; it is not the same as telling others what to do, and not the same as deciding faster. Reading organisation as dominance and empathy as weakness turns a preference into a character judgement.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
In a reputational incident both may have said "hold off publishing", and both will pull up what has already gone out to check it. That resemblance is easily remembered as the same kind of steadiness, when it comes more from the shared J and from the post — anyone sitting in an outward-facing role, of any type, will be asked to think before speaking.

The shared J only says both tend to form an arrangement outward; it does not say what the arrangement is built on. The three differences are read separately: E/I is whether attention and energy turn outward or inward more often; S/N is whether sourcing trusts facts and experience, or notices connections and possibility faster; T/F is whether the judgement weighs a consistently applicable standard, or people and values. The three cannot substitute for each other, and "who moves first" cannot stand in for any of them.

### The same negative comment, two usable entry points

In this fictional example, a widely shared post says a product broke after two months and customer support failed to help. The company has full support records and can deliver a resolution within three days.

One entry point is the checkable record: which order this user placed, how long the first support reply took, what result can be delivered within how many days. The other looks for patterns across the replies: are people reporting a product fault, feeling dismissed by support, or both? This illustrates an S/N contrast in the use of information. Either person can check the records and look for recurring concerns, and neither approach identifies someone’s type.

Both entry points have costs. Checking only the facts may produce a statement read as a work report, with the anger intact; reading only the feeling may promise what cannot be delivered. A workable order is to spend an hour confirming what can be checked, then use those facts to calibrate the tone; the two do not need two people, and who does which part follows the information, authority and duty at the time.

Order is not a criterion. An ESTJ who has worked support or communications may weigh tone first, and an INFJ who has handled many incidents may pull the timeline first; the reverse is also common. The scene shows which kind of basis each cites more often; it does not show who cares more about people.

### No position shares a name — what is shared is the four kinds of process

In the four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and INFJ is Ni–Fe–Ti–Se: ESTJ leads with Te, auxiliary Si, third Ne, inferior Fi; INFJ leads with Ni, auxiliary Fe, third Ti, inferior Se. No position shares a name.

Both stacks include Thinking, Feeling, Sensing and Intuition. The exact labels differ because each function is directed inward in one stack and outward in the other, and the order also changes: ESTJ puts judging outward (Te) and perceiving inward (Si); INFJ integrates perceptually inward first (Ni) and judges outward (Fe).

What each position more often handles: Te writes standards and results into an executable, checkable form; Si compares the present situation with past experience and precedent; Ne moves from one thing to other explanations and other possibilities; Fi lets a judgement carry the values one holds. Ni integrates scattered clues into a pattern or a direction; Fe reads the feelings of those present and the shared understanding between them; Ti checks whether a set of statements is internally consistent; Se takes the facts available to the senses right now.

Whether the third position is labelled introverted or extraverted is not consistent across tables: for ESTJ's Ne and INFJ's Ti, some tables give only the function name without settling an attitude. This page uses the common writing and does not present it as the Foundation's only version; the disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain who cares more about others. A position is an emphasis in the model, and does not show who is better at which kind of work, whether a collaboration runs smoothly, or who attracts whom. Both base descriptions are the [ESTJ profile](/en/personality/estj) and the [INFJ profile](/en/personality/infj).

sections.body_md:
The table fixes the same comment, the same public information, the same handling authority and the same response window. Change the authority, the deadline or the legal risk and both columns change. Both types can use both approaches; the table records only which basis is taken first more often.

| The same stage (one comment, one set of information) | ESTJ: the basis more likely attended to | INFJ: the basis more likely attended to | What this row corresponds to |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Which parts of the comment are worth checking first | The order record, the interval between support replies, how far the after-sales process actually got | The wording that recurs in the comment and the replies, and whether the complaint points at quality or at attitude | S/N: sourcing from facts and experience, or from pattern and possibility |
| Whether to apologise publicly, and how far to go | Whether responsibility is established, where the commitment ends, how it will be measured afterwards | Whether the person wants this sentence, or a concrete remedy and a change in practice | T/F: judging by a consistent standard, or by people and values |
| What the first paragraph of the statement says | Use a consistent standard for deciding which confirmed details to include in the opening | Weigh which of those same confirmed details matter most to the affected customer | T/F: same facts, standard first or situation first |
| What time to publish, and who signs | Wait until approval is complete and the wording is unified, then give a time that can be met | Wait until the accounts align and the tone cannot be read as deflection | Shared J: both tend to form an arrangement, on different bases |
| How to handle the second wave | Check concrete claims, timestamps and corrections in the same replies | Look for patterns across those same replies and what they might mean | S/N: sourcing decides which layer is filled first |
| What the review looks at | Which link in the process failed, and how the response time limit should change | Whether this relationship can be repaired, and how to open the next conversation | Under the shared J, sourcing and judging differ in emphasis |

A public-facing assignment cannot establish E/I. To reflect on that preference, compare settings with similar responsibilities where each person could work through the same information in discussion or in private. The timing of a public reply tells you little about that choice.

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. An ESTJ with ten years in support will also weigh tone first, and an INFJ handling a first incident may only know to go through the records; the same person also changes approach with the scope of authority, a manager's requirement and the cost of delay, so these rows cannot be used to classify.
sections.title: ESTJ and INFJ in one minute

sections.body_md:
Scope note: what follows is how the two organise information and divide the work inside one fictional incident. It does not cover legal characterisation, crisis-handling procedure or the specific scale of a public commitment. Anything touching the law is for legal counsel; when a public line is needed, follow the company's approval and compliance process.

Working together, the two easily get stuck where there is no agreement on what is actually being solved, and the statement has already gone out. That is usually a matter of collaborative rhythm, not of type pairing.

The division is assigned by authority, experience and current duty, and either type can do any part: fact-checking, the limits of a commitment, wording and follow-up communication all need a second pair of eyes. When publication needs delaying, write down three things: what is still being checked, the latest point at which a decision must be made, and whether a short progress note should go out first.

### A public reply to one negative comment

(Fictional scene.) The same matter admits two equally acceptable pieces of writing. One sets out the check results and the actions: when the user bought, that the first reply took more than forty-eight hours, that a replacement has been arranged with shipping refunded, and that the response time limit now sits in performance reviews. The other acknowledges the situation first: that a user was only heard after being passed around repeatedly is itself a failure, and a replacement is only the floor.

The first offers an account that can be checked; the second offers an attitude that can be believed. Publish only the first and readers know the process changed while the anger remains; only the second and readers find it agreeable but cannot tell what actually changed. Either type can write either version; the difference is which kind of basis is thought of first.

The check can be a read-through: show both versions to a few readers outside the company and ask three questions each — which facts did you see, which commitment did you remember, and do you think the other side's dissatisfaction was answered. The feedback reports the effect of the text; it does not verify the writer's type or function preference, and cannot show who is better suited to writing statements.

### A friend is being piled on in the comments

(Fictional scene.) A friend's opinion trends and the comments are full of personal attacks. What can be done falls into two kinds: operational — do not reply yet, save screenshots, appeal to the platform if needed, put together a timeline; and companionable — call first, let them talk it out, then ask "do you want me to say something publicly".

Both can go wrong: only the operational makes the person feel alone, and only the comforting leaves the actual harm continuing. Either type may do either first, and either may do both.

A workable move is to ask the friend which kind of help they want, and to make "I will not speak for you" an explicit option. Speaking for someone looks loyal but can spread the fire to two people; whether to respond publicly is the person's own decision.

### New material appears late at night

(Fictional scene.) Four hours after the statement goes out, someone posts a recording of a support call whose tone is worse than the written record. Three pieces of information work can be done: obtain the full recording, confirm whether it was edited, and judge whether it is a new fact or new evidence of the same fact.

The nature changes where the reply lands: if it is a new fact, acknowledge first that this was not known, then add; if it is new evidence of the same fact, the point is why it was not stated clearly before. If the deadline is already tight and media are pressing, either type may put out a short note first and fill in detail later. The most common failure in a panic is meeting feeling with process language — that has nothing to do with type and everything to do with how prepared you were.

sections.body_md:
"Who is more decisive" cannot be evidence. ESTJ decides fast when information is complete and authority is clear, and INFJ is equally unhurried when the direction is clear; conversely, both are cautious when the facts are unclear. Speed is a product of circumstance and experience.

"Who is colder" is also a misreading. ESTJ's Fi sitting fourth does not mean not caring about people, only that it is not often the first basis for a judgement; INFJ's Fe sitting second, in the auxiliary, does not mean having no principles. A position describes emphasis, not how much anyone cares.

The third misread is taking J as a need to control or a short temper. J describes forming an arrangement outward first; it is not the same as telling others what to do, and not the same as deciding faster. Reading organisation as dominance and empathy as weakness turns a preference into a character judgement.

The fourth is settling a type from one performance. "Check facts first" and "read the feeling first" can both appear in either type, and the same person switches sides in different settings. Classifying on one sighting usually gets it wrong.

The fifth is taking a job for a type. People in support, communications or incident response are trained into a fixed set of moves; that is the result of training, not a change of preference.

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, confirm whether it was the same questionnaire: the item bank, language version and scoring convention. Different versions are not compared directly, and the result cannot be read backwards into "I must have acted first".

Then go through the three axes item by item: how you read them, and the situation you answered from. Were you responsible for outward accountability during that period, were you doing work that required reading people's feelings over a long stretch, had you just been publicly questioned. A role pushes a person toward one end, and that pull is worth recording.

The practice can be arranged like this: take a few recent occasions when you had to answer someone's dissatisfaction, and write four lines for each — what evidence you had, what your role and authority allowed you to do, which judging standards you considered, and whether another setting would have changed the weighing. If "is the standard consistent" or "what does this mean for the people involved" keeps appearing, it is worth discussing as your habit; it is reflection material, not a typing rule, and no threshold of occasions is set.

When results stay inconsistent over time, do not substitute a source of fatigue for the assessment. If the item bank reports dimension scores, look at which of E/I, S/N and T/F sit nearer the boundary; without dimension scores or scoring notes, do not infer a boundary, and no retest interval is prescribed.

items.answer:
In the fictional complaint, either person can check the support timeline and look for recurring concerns across the replies. S/N describes the distinction between specific observations and wider patterns. T/F describes whether a decision gives more weight to consistent criteria or to the needs and values of people affected.

The shared J only says both tend to push matters to a state that can be accounted for, not what they judge by. Both can start from either end, and the order depends on duty, deadline, information and what the person involved wants; labelling "checks facts first" as ESTJ misses a great many counterexamples.
items.question: With one negative comment in front of them, what does each more often seize on?

items.answer:
No. Beyond T/F they also differ on E/I and S/N, while J is shared.

The three ask different things: E/I asks whether attention and energy turn outward or inward more often; S/N asks whether sourcing trusts facts and experience, or notices connections and possibility faster; T/F asks whether judgement weighs a consistently applicable standard, or people and values. On the same comment, S/N describes which kinds of information may get more weight, while T/F describes the criteria each person may weigh in a decision; and the public-reply setting alone cannot resolve E/I.
items.question: Is it all a T/F difference? Where does the judgement start for each?

items.answer:
They are not counterexamples, and need no exception to explain: both performances can appear in either type.

Ability, training and the duty of the moment all rewrite performance, and that belongs to skill and circumstance, not to a change of preference. What discriminates better is which kind of basis is cited more often across comparable situations; a single performance, one phrasing or the order on one evening cannot settle a type.
items.question: INFJ can be brisk and ESTJ can be considerate — are those counterexamples?

items.answer:
Not by type. Assign by authority, experience and the division at the time, and either type can do any part.

In practice, fact-checking, the limits of a commitment, calibration of wording and follow-up communication all deserve a second pair of eyes. To practise, take one fictional statement, have one person write the facts section and the other the attitude section, then read them together; who writes which can be swapped, and the reading looks at which section lacks evidence and which lacks a response.
items.question: In a communications incident, which part does each own?

items.answer:
A commitment not delivered, or an action and its progress not explained clearly.

Both damage trust on either side and have nothing to do with type. One method is to write every commitment as a checkable sentence: who, by when, delivers what. A sentence that cannot be written that way does not go into the statement; discussing the wording afterwards is less trouble than fixing the tone first and adding facts later.
items.question: What most easily damages trust when ESTJ and INFJ work together?

items.answer:
Check whether it was the same questionnaire and version, then look at the role and situation before and after each round.

If your role requires public communication or sustained support for someone else, you may answer with those duties in mind. That alone does not tell you which way the result will move. Then go through E/I, S/N and T/F item by item: how you read them, and what state you were in when answering; do not substitute "is my fatigue from things or from relationships" for an interpretation of the assessment — that is only another clue.
